_about: The reasoning behind the route, for the Route page. Every claim comes from docs/research (00-synthesis, 01-events, 02-closures, 03-transport, 05-north-west, 06-south-west-hokkaido, 07-lodging, 08-pregnancy; researched 1 Oct 2026) and docs/research/plan-doc (12–13 Oct 2026). Sources are the ones those files cite.
intro: Japan has 47 prefectures and hundreds of towns worth a week. We looked at the whole country for these exact 21 days: what is open, what is closed, which trains sell out, where the snow is, what is sensible at 29–32 weeks of pregnancy, and which places can sleep seven. Twenty-six regions made the long list. The New Year calendar and the pregnancy ruled most of them out before taste came into it. Tap any area to see what it is known for, what it is like in late December and early January, and why it is in or out.

facts.title: New Year closes most of Japan for a week
facts.text: Between 29 Dec and 3 Jan museums, castles, markets and most independent restaurants close. Shrines, temples, onsen towns and department-store food halls (from 2 Jan) stay open. Trains are fullest on 27–30 Dec leaving Tokyo and 2–4 Jan coming back; JR East puts the peaks on 30 Dec and 3 Jan. The two calm travel days are 31 Dec and 1 Jan. And 9 Jan starts a three-day weekend, so the last night should be close to the airport. That gives any sensible trip the same shape: Tokyo first, move before the 28th, sit still somewhere self-sufficient over New Year, move on the quiet day, finish within reach of Tokyo.

facts.title: Fernanda will be 29 to 32 weeks pregnant
facts.text: Standard advice for the third trimester, and what her doctor and the airline ask for, shape the trip more than anything else: keep moving days to about four hours door to door with one long train, take it easy the day after a long move, walk a comfortable distance with places to sit, avoid long queues and standing events, avoid icy paths and stone stairs without a handrail, use onsen only in a private bath, short and not too hot, and stay within reach of a hospital with 24-hour obstetrics. In practice that takes out bus-only mountain villages for the nights, long domestic flights, Hokkaido's icy pavements and the famous temple-bell queues. It is also why most stays are two nights or more and the afternoons are kept light. None of this is a rule she has to follow; it is the default, and she decides on the day.

facts.title: Winter helps in some places and not in others
facts.text: On the Sea of Japan side (Shirakawa-go, Takayama, the Nagano hills) snow on the ground is near-certain by 25 Dec. Kanazawa and the cities get cold with some snow. The Fuji side is dry, sunny and at its clearest of the year: Fuji is fully visible on about six January mornings in ten. The famous winter events all come after we leave: the Shirakawa-go light-up (11–31 Jan), the Sapporo and Otaru snow festivals (February), the Zao snow monsters at full size (late January), Ginzan Onsen at its best. Chasing them in our dates means cold without the show. So the route goes where December actually delivers: thatched houses in snow on the way to Takayama, crab at its peak in Kanazawa, a ryokan New Year, and Fuji in its clearest month.

route.intro: Put those three together and the route almost draws itself. Here is why each stop is where it is, in this order.

steps.title: Tokyo first, 4 nights
steps.text: The flights land here. The first days absorb the jet lag and give the four first-timers the classic city while the Christmas lights are still on (they end 25 Dec). Museums are open before the 29th; Monday the 21st is their closing day, so that becomes the market-and-gardens day.

steps.title: Kanazawa, 4 nights, done by the 27th
steps.text: Two and a half hours on the Hokuriku shinkansen, booked before the 27 Dec rush. Kanazawa is the slow middle of the trip: a whole house with a kitchen and a washing machine, the 21st Century Museum, Kenroku-en with its snow ropes, the geisha and samurai districts, and the female kobako crab in the last week of its season. Museums close on Monday 28 Dec and from the 29th, so four nights put the three museum days before that.

steps.title: Shirakawa-go on the way, not as a base
steps.text: The Nohi bus from Kanazawa stops in the thatched village for two and a half hours and continues to Takayama. No farmhouse takes a group of seven over New Year, the inns have steep stairs and shared baths, and the village light-ups are in late January. A stop on the bus gives the snow village without any of that.

steps.title: Takayama, 2 nights
steps.text: The old town, the morning market, the sake breweries and Hida beef fill one full day. The Jinya closes on 29 Dec, so we see it on arrival. Two nights, not more: the town is a one-day place, and a third day while its museums are shut would be slow.

steps.title: Gero for New Year's Eve, 2 nights
steps.text: The move from Takayama is 45 minutes, so the two worst travel days of the year hold no long train for us. A ryokan includes the New Year's Eve dinner and the New Year breakfast on 1 Jan, which matters because restaurants close. Gero is flat, has footbaths, and sits on the line to Kyoto.

steps.title: Kyoto on New Year's Day, 4 nights
steps.text: 1 Jan is the quiet day on the trains, so that is when we go. Kyoto's museums reopen on 2 Jan, the city is in its New Year rituals, and Nara goes on Monday the 4th when Kyoto's museums close again. A house with a living room covers the evenings while most restaurants are still shut.

steps.title: Kawaguchiko, 2 nights, Fuji across the lake
steps.text: From the north shore of Lake Kawaguchi, Fuji stands straight across the water with nothing in the way: from the room, the promenade, the ropeway and the boat. Early January is its clearest month, and the place is new for all seven of us. The move from Kyoto is the longest of the trip, about four and a quarter hours by shinkansen to Mishima and the Fujikyu bus, on 5 Jan when the New Year rush is over. A lake hotel with beds and a lift, one full day for the ropeway and the boat, two dawns to catch the mountain clear, and a hospital with obstetrics in Fujiyoshida. Then two hours on the Fuji Excursion train straight into Shinjuku, which keeps the last nights near the airport.

steps.title: Tokyo again, 2 nights
steps.text: The museums that were closed in December (the Musée d'Orsay show, the Tokyo National Museum open late on Friday 8 Jan), the shopping, the farewell dinner, and a buffer before a Saturday flight on a holiday weekend.

for_whom.who: João, Carolina and Tatiana, first time in Japan
for_whom.text: You get the three everyone should see first: Tokyo, Kyoto and Fuji. On top of that, three things most first visits miss: a snow village, a samurai city with the best garden in the country, and a real ryokan New Year with the temple bell at midnight. The fuller alternative (eight bases) adds Hiroshima and the snow baths if you would rather see more and rest less.

for_whom.who: Carlos and Nadir, first time, very fit
for_whom.text: The classic sights without the exhaustion. One big thing a day, done in the morning when the sights are quietest; a long lunch; the afternoon free to keep going or not. Beds and lifts wherever we sleep, rooms with beds at the ryokan, and no day over about 10 km unless you want it.

for_whom.who: Pedro and Fernanda, who know Tokyo and Kyoto
for_whom.text: Five of the seven stops are new to you: Kanazawa, Shirakawa-go, Takayama, Gero and Kawaguchiko. You have done Hakone, so the Fuji stop is the lake instead, with the mountain straight across the water, new for everyone. The two cities you know are the two the first-timers need most, and in Kyoto you get the New Year rites you have not seen.

The route was shaped around you: moves of about four hours or less (the longest, Kyoto to the lake, is about four and a quarter), one long journey a day, an easy day after each, private baths, light afternoons, and the right to drop any plan on the day. None of it is binding; it is the default. The one place the route goes against the medical advice is New Year's Eve: the advice is to spend those nights in a city with a perinatal centre, and Gero is a small spa town 1.5–2.5 h from Kyoto. We accepted that for the ryokan New Year. If your doctor would rather not, the clean alternative is the Kyoto house from 30 Dec, and the gentler alternative keeps the night in Takayama instead.

not_chosen.intro: Everything below is good. It is out because of travel time, the New Year calendar or the pregnancy. Several come back as other routes to look at.

items.why: The other Fuji base: five art museums for a cloudy day, ryokan with a private bath in every room, an hour closer to Kyoto and 80 minutes from Shinjuku. Pedro and Fernanda have done it, and Fuji shows over the ridges rather than straight across the water.
Snow monkeys and an onsen street, but it costs a Tokyo day and Kanazawa's rest day, and the forest path can be icy.
Naoshima's art and Korakuen fit after Kyoto, at the price of Kawaguchiko and the Fuji mornings.
A lovely crab-and-baths town, but it repeats Kanazawa's crab and Gero's onsen, and the way home is 5–6 hours.
Open-air baths in deep snow and a ropeway to 2,156 m, but it makes New Year's Day a five-hour travel day and the summit deck is icy.
items.comeback: a day trip from Takayama, or the fuller alternative

items.why: Important history and Miyajima, but a long westward leg and two more nights.

The best snow and a flight each way, but the Sapporo and Otaru festivals are in February, the ice underfoot is the one thing to avoid at 30 weeks, and it is the most expensive lodging in Japan at New Year.
The most photographed snowy onsen street, but far north, day visits are capped, and its few small inns book a year ahead.
A steaming hot-water field, but the water is too hot and acidic for Fernanda and it is a long way from Kyoto.
A temple night with the dawn fire ritual is memorable, but the lodgings are cold, the beds are floor futons and the paths are icy.
Yufuin, Kurokawa and Takachiho need a car or a bus that runs one to three times a day; the Aso crater is closed; sand baths refuse pregnant guests.
Longer transfers, colder, fewer houses for seven, and its festivals are in February.
The Iya vine bridges close December to March.
Flights and boats; boats are not advised for Fernanda.
Lacquered shrines in a cedar forest, but hundreds of icy stone stairs in winter.

points: We looked across the whole country in early October 2026: events, closures, trains, places to stay and what is sensible in the third trimester, and 156 experiences, each with a note on how well it suits Fernanda. The route and the five region guides followed on 12–13 October.

Most 2026–27 year-end calendars were not published in October, so many opening hours follow the 2025–26 pattern. Where a date is confirmed (the Nozomi all-reserved window, Takashimaya's 1–2 Jan closure, the Ekiden dates) it says so. We recheck everything in December.
Prices are estimates: lodging at the mid tier for seven with a New Year uplift, fares for reserved seats, food by pace. Treat the budget as plus or minus 15 percent.
Every place, restaurant and opening time links to the page it came from. If a claim has no link, treat it as our opinion.
The taste calls are ours: that four nights in Kanazawa beat five in Takayama, that a ryokan New Year beats a city one. The facts narrowed the field; those calls are for the family to make together.
